# The Turning

The world's oracular deck. It is emphatically not our tarot — a different artifact with a
different history, ratified whole in D-0148 and woken from the world's own substrate by the
tarot-remap method (D-0147). Everyday folk usage calls it the Turning; the name drifts by
region, as the thing itself does.

## What it is
> status: ratified (D-0146, D-0148, D-0180)

The Turning began as a reckoning-game of the old commons — a way to teach and settle the
arithmetic of Frith, made small enough for a child's hands ([[wyrd-and-frith]]). It turned to
counsel because its painted leaves already held the standing premises of the world, so a person
learned to deal them against their own tangle instead of against an opponent. Laid as a spread,
the leaves hold a problem still and free the mind for the argument itself: the same extended
cognition as the knot and the woven record ([[artifacts-and-memory]], D-0028). Its shape is a
wheel, never a ladder — no leaf outranks another — so a reading asks where on the turn a thing
stands and which way it moves, the deliberate inverse of tarot's climb toward Death. That one
structural choice carries the world's whole thesis in an object: the world gets things right,
then wrong, then right again, and agency turns the wheel ([[cycles]], D-0040).
Within the one-proof architecture, the Turning is a premise map and counsel interface.
It helps a person find, hold, and reorder premises; it is not an independent magical
engine.

## Counsel, never prophecy
> status: ratified (D-0146, D-0180)

A reading is counsel. Laying the querent's own premises where the eye can walk them, a reader
returns a better question, never a fixed future — divination kept inside the world's epistemology,
where the Wyrd is accumulated consequence and not prophecy. Skill is joiner-skill: a good reader
lays a spread that discomforts productively, and a lazy or dishonest one flatters. A bad reading
is bad work, not bad luck. See [[artifacts-and-memory]] "Divination as counsel" for the doctrine
across all the world's card-kin.
This non-prophetic floor is part of the hard-magic contract. The deck can reveal a
question, contradiction, missing premise, or dishonest framing; it does not tell fate.

## The anatomy — Grounds, Hands, Weathers, and the Reckoner
> status: ratified (D-0148)

The deck is built from the spoken proof's own parts and organised as a round. Four layers:

- **The Grounds** — the commons-domains where taking and giving happen, and the subject a reading
  is *about* (a leaf is a holdable premise, the grounds of an argument). The shared lowlands deck
  keeps four — the Wood, the Water, the Field, the Hearth — and the set is region-variable canon:
  a salt-fringe deck reckons in the Tide and the Catch, a crag deck in the Ore and the Fell, a
  richer deck adds the Fold (beasts) and the Stone (the boundary, the deep past). The suits drift
  with the commons they serve, the way Mamluk polo-sticks became European batons.
- **The Hands** — four working roles of the Frith-cycle, and the agent acting on a Ground: the
  **Taker** draws from the commons, the **Keeper** holds the saved thing, the **Giver** returns
  it, the **Mender** repairs the wear. These are moments of the law and carry no social rank, so
  the court cards themselves teach the round of take, keep, give back, mend. Their faces are
  folk-figures that drift by region (below).
- **The Weathers** — the Wyrd's cyclical conditions, the not-fate weather that falls on any Ground.
  Twelve of them, as four reciprocal pairs and four passages: the Greening and the Rot; the Flood
  and the Dearth; the Binding and the Loosing (the *geas* register); the Mending and the Sundering
  (the torn-and-regathered axis, D-0138); then the Road, the Bourn (the threshold, hedge against
  wall, D-0144), the Debt (axiomatic debt come due), and the Fallow (the held-back field, rest and
  waiting). They form a closed ring with no highest card: the Rot leads back round to the Greening,
  and a reading never asks what conquers what.
- **The Reckoner** — the one leaf that is neither subject nor agent nor condition. It is the
  querent's own standpoint at the hub of the round, so every reading implicates the one who lays
  it. It is the anti-Fool: a still centre that must choose which way to turn, never an innocent
  stepping off a cliff.

**A count from the world's own sky.** Four Grounds (sixteen Hands) with twelve Weathers and the
Reckoner make twenty-nine leaves — one for each night of the moon's turning. That count comes from
the tide-and-moon craft timing, not from tarot's seventy-eight, and a full deck "runs the moon."
Because the Grounds drift, the exact count varies by region, and that variability is itself canon.

## The reading practice
> status: ratified (D-0146, D-0148)

A reading is an argument laid where the eye can walk it. The reader deals the Ground in play, the
Hand or Hands upon it, and the Weather it stands under, all arranged around the Reckoner, and then
walks the querent around the laid wheel until the real question surfaces. Layouts carry names,
because a layout is the shape of an argument: **a round** (three leaves, the everyday deal), **the
whole round** (the full turn), **the ford** (a crossing or a decision), and **the debt-square**
(laid to find, in a grievance, who truly owes whom). The debt-square is the reading the licensed
decks cannot deal (below).

## The figures, and the deck as archetype library
> status: ratified (D-0147, D-0148)

The Hands carry the archetypal loads; their faces are dormant folk-figures woken onto the grid,
each carrying a Frith-load, each drifting by region while the load holds. The Taker wears the
Fowler, the Reaper, or the Tithe-man; the Keeper wears the Drover, the Seed-keeper, or the Warden;
the Giver wears the Fen-wife, the Host, or the Sower; the Mender wears the Smith in the crags, the
Pleacher in the lowlands hedgerows, the Net-mender on the fringes. A few Weathers that a folk-figure
already fits carry a face too — the Keener rides the Sundering, the Ferryman carries the Road, the
Gleaner keeps the Fallow — while most Weathers stay bare conditions, which keeps the wheel from
filling up with a pantheon.

Because every figure sits at a known cell — a Hand, on a Ground, under a Weather — the grid is a
generator, and the world adopts it as the writers'-room situation-grammar (D-0147). A single cell
is a casting call: *the Taker on the Field under the Debt* is a tithe-bailiff in a debt-soured
farming spoke, his dramatic function already loaded. A whole spread is a dramatic situation, a
specific reciprocity-imbalance to be read and mended. It runs both ways: designing the deck figures
generates cast and setting, and new regional cast feeds fresh faces back into the deck, so the
thing the characters use to read their world is the thing the writers use to build it. Even the core
party sites cleanly on the grid, the proof it works — Geir is the Mender on the Ore under
the Debt; the apprentice is the Keeper on the Tide under the Loosing; Enfys moves from the Sundering
toward the Mending; the Plenty is the Taker that never becomes a Giver, the broken Frith-cycle in a
single leaf, the whole allegory carried without a word of allegory.

## The lineage — eight hundred years of thumbprints
> status: ratified (D-0148)

The deck should feel handled. It is game-first and oracle-late: elders still play the old
give-and-take game for buttons, children learn Frith on it before they can read, and a
cunning-woman reading for a frightened village and two crag-men gambling debts on a stump reach for
the same leaves. It drifts by region the way the economy does — a Corsbach deck and a Halspetra deck
share the Hands and the Weathers while their Grounds and even their faces differ — so a travelling
reader re-learns the local suits as the party re-learns each region's economy. It survived the
memory-purges (D-0072): the empire burned decks as "reckoning-witchery", yet they are painted on
any scrap and cost nothing, so they could not be burned out, and when books were policed a drover
carried the commons' whole reasoning-grammar in a coat pocket, dismissed as a card-game. The deck
is the layfolk's surviving library ([[information-control]], [[cycles]]).

### Misprints that became meanings
> status: proposed

Colour, not yet ratified: the tradition metabolises its own errors. A cracked woodblock once split
the Mender's hands, and for three generations a whole valley read that leaf as the Broken-Handed,
the wound that teaches, until the misprint was a real card with its own honest meaning. A slipped
stencil bled the Greening's green across the Rot, and a border parish still deals them as one leaf,
the Turning-of-the-year.

### The deep-time stratum
> status: proposed

Colour, not yet ratified: the anchor's spade turns up a bog-preserved deck of a prior age whose
Grounds name commons that no longer exist — a leaf for a drowned valley, a Hand for a craft gone
extinct — proof the game outlived a whole world ([[cycles]]). One of the protagonist's absorbed
voices played the game in an earlier cycle and reads with a dead grammar, so she carries a
deck-history in her own head.

## The keep-stamped deck — a tool for the mind inverted into a cage
> status: ratified (D-0148)

Unable to ban the leaves, the empire sells them instead: clean, keep-stamped decks, the
respectable household's deck. Their Grounds are pre-sorted and their hard Weathers are cut out —
no Debt, no Sundering, no Bourn — so a frightened person laying them can never reach the
debt-square, never arrive at the question of who owes what to whom. Every reading soothes. It is
the extended-cognition doctrine turned against itself: the empire's idea of a tool for thinking is
a device for *not* thinking, and it is marketed as a kindness. It is the deck-scale form of the
false curriculum ([[information-control]]) and a keep-stamped good like any other ([[economy]]).
One guardrail governs every scene that uses it: the rig stays subtext, discovered and never
announced — the moment a character says it aloud, the thing becomes a wink and dies.

## Enfys's practice
> status: ratified (D-0148)

Enfys reads as an imperial-trained defector re-learning the folk way ([[protagonist]]). Raised in
the chalk core, she first learned the rigorous, premise-chained scribe's reading, very likely on a
keep-stamped deck; her Moses arc is literally the re-painting of the empire's sorted Grounds back
into honest ones, on stolen scraped vellum in soot-and-bog-berry ink ([[arts]]). The cunning-woman's
reading is warmer and more intuitive, and a drover's is a two-leaf glance at a sky — the same deck
carrying three literacies, the chalk-literate inverse of the knot-literacy the apprentice already
embodies.

## Introduction and reveal
> status: ratified (D-0148, D-0155)

Design sketch, not yet ratified — D-0148 commissions it: the deck's rules surface across many
small plot beats, never an infodump. The apprentice meets it first as a children's game before
anyone calls it counsel; the debt-square arrives only when a grievance needs it; and the rig in the
keep-stamped deck is felt as wrongness long before it is understood. The full reveal ladder — which
beat teaches which rule, in what order — is worked out in `docs/proposals/DP-001-turning-reveal-ladder.md`.
